title: Negotiating Ontological Boundaries in User-Authored Personal Sensing Systems
gist: An Apple/Stanford HCI paper reports a week-long Wizard of Oz study in which people trained personalized ML sensing systems on phenomena they defined themselves. It identifies four sites where participants negotiated what the system's categories mean. The page also carries teasers for two unrelated Apple papers.

insights.claim: The authors argue that designed artifacts are ontological: they shape and sometimes limit what people can imagine or do, and giving people authorship over how systems are built is one way to reduce such foreclosure.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Signals Apple research interest in user-defined, personalized on-device ML rather than fixed vendor-defined categories.
insights.quote: Designed artifacts are ontological, shaping, and at times limiting, what becomes possible or imaginable.

insights.claim: Prior systems that let users author their own tools are usually judged on usability, usefulness or technical feasibility, which leaves the negotiation of ontological boundaries unexamined.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Points to an evaluation gap in personalization products that could shape future design criteria.

insights.claim: The study used two open-ended probes with a Wizard of Oz technique, simulating the experience of training a personalized ML system on phenomena users define themselves, with participants using one probe in everyday life for a week.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: The system was simulated, not a working product, so findings are exploratory and not evidence of technical capability.

insights.claim: Participants negotiated ontological boundaries at four sites: the boundaries of a phenomenon, the subject as part of relations, what counts as signal versus noise, and the objectivity of data.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Gives a checklist of where user-defined sensing products will face friction: label definitions, social context, noise filtering and trust in data.
insights.quote: the boundaries of a phenomena, the subject as part of relations, what is signal and what is noise, and the objectivity of data

insights.claim: The authors propose open-ended probes as a method for ontological design and offer starting points for supporting boundary negotiation through design.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Qualitative research output, with no commercial or performance claim.

themes.theme: Page context and related Apple work

insights.claim: The paper was authored by Apple-affiliated and Stanford researchers (including Gierad Laput and James Landay), and some authors did the work while at Apple.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Shows continuing Apple-Stanford HCI collaboration on personal sensing.

insights.claim: A related Apple paper accepted at ARES 2026 warns that autonomous negotiation agents deployed in high-stakes settings like insurance and procurement face a subtler threat that cryptographic protection of disclosed constraint values does not address.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Hints at emerging security concerns for agent-to-agent negotiation, though only a teaser is shown.
insights.locator: Autonomous negotiation agents are increasingly deployed

insights.claim: Apple's ODKE+ is described as a production-grade system that automatically extracts and ingests millions of open-domain facts from web sources with high precision to keep knowledge graphs fresh and complete.
insights.speaker: Apple ML Research
insights.so_what: Indicates Apple runs production knowledge-graph automation, though only a teaser is shown.
